Documentation should explain why the feature does not change the basic lending character of the cash flows.
Study instruction:
- For a modified-rate instrument, document the feature, the benchmark cash flows and the basis for concluding that the effect is not significant.
Key point:
- Some limited contractual modifications can remain consistent with SPPI.
- The entity must substantiate the assessment rather than assume that every minor-looking feature is acceptable.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: 2024 Amendments to Classification and Measurement of Financial Instruments
29. Q: How are equity investments classified under IFRS 9?
A: Show answer
Equity investments are generally measured at FVPL unless the entity makes an irrevocable election at initial recognition to present fair-value changes in OCI for an investment that is not held for trading and is not contingent consideration in a business combination. Under this FVOCI election, cumulative gains and losses remain in OCI and are not recycled to profit or loss when the investment is disposed of. Dividends are generally recognised in profit or loss unless they clearly represent a recovery of part of the cost of the investment. The equity FVOCI category is therefore different from debt FVOCI: it does not use the business-model and SPPI tests, and it is not subject to the expected-credit-loss impairment model described for debt instruments.
Study instruction:
- Check whether the equity investment is held for trading and document any irrevocable FVOCI designation made at initial recognition.
Key point:
- Qualifying non-trading equity investments may be irrevocably designated at FVOCI.
- Equity FVOCI gains and losses are not recycled to profit or loss on disposal.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
30. Q: How are financial liabilities classified under IFRS 9?
A: Show answer
The chapter identifies two principal measurement categories: financial liabilities at amortised cost and financial liabilities at FVPL. Liabilities held for trading, including derivative financial liabilities, fall into FVPL. An entity may also designate a liability at FVPL at initial recognition when doing so eliminates or significantly reduces a measurement or recognition inconsistency, subject to the standard's requirements. Liabilities that do not fall into the FVPL category are generally measured at amortised cost. The classification approach for liabilities is not the same as the business-model and SPPI approach used for financial assets, so entities should not apply the asset classification matrix mechanically to liabilities.
Study instruction:
- Classify a derivative liability, a trading short position, a bond payable and an ordinary trade creditor using the liability rules.
Key point:
- Financial liabilities are generally measured at amortised cost or FVPL.
- The financial-asset business-model and SPPI tests do not determine liability classification.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
31. Q: How is the own-credit-risk component treated for a financial liability designated at FVPL?
A: Show answer
For a financial liability designated at FVPL that is not held for trading, the portion of the fair-value gain or loss attributable to changes in the issuer's own credit risk is normally presented in OCI. This avoids the counterintuitive outcome in which deterioration in the issuer's credit standing produces a gain in profit or loss. However, if presenting the own-credit component in OCI creates or enlarges an accounting mismatch in profit or loss, the chapter explains that the gains and losses are presented entirely in profit or loss. The entity therefore needs to identify the own-credit component separately and assess the accounting-mismatch condition rather than automatically placing every fair-value movement in OCI.
Study instruction:
- Reconcile the total fair-value movement into own-credit and other market components and document whether an accounting mismatch exception applies.
Key point:
- Own-credit movements on qualifying designated liabilities normally go to OCI.
- The accounting-mismatch exception can require all gains and losses to remain in profit or loss.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
32. Q: When may financial assets be reclassified under IFRS 9?
A: Show answer
Reclassification of non-derivative debt financial assets is required only when an entity changes its business model for managing those assets, and such changes are expected to be very rare. A qualifying change may arise when an entity acquires or disposes of a business or fundamentally changes the way a portfolio is managed. Gradual changes in management practice do not automatically mean that existing assets are reclassified; assets already held remain in their original category when a business model evolves over time, while new assets are classified under the new model. Equity instruments designated at FVOCI and financial liabilities are not reclassified. Certain changes related to hedge designation or credit-exposure measurement are not treated as reclassifications.
Study instruction:
- Distinguish a genuine portfolio-level business-model change from ordinary asset sales, changes in intent or routine management activity.
Key point:
- Reclassification is rare and driven by a genuine change in the business model.
- It is not a tool for managing reported gains and losses opportunistically.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
33. Q: When does an entity recognise a financial asset or financial liability under IFRS 9?
A: Show answer
An entity recognises a financial asset or financial liability when, and only when, it becomes a party to the contractual provisions of the instrument. Unconditional trade receivables and payables are recognised when the entity obtains the contractual right to receive cash or obligation to pay it. A forward contract within IFRS 9 is recognised when the entity becomes a party to the contract, even though its initial net fair value may be zero because the rights and obligations offset at inception. An option is recognised when the holder or writer becomes a party to it. Planned future transactions, however likely, are not recognised as financial assets or liabilities before the entity becomes party to a qualifying contract. Certain firm commitments involving non-financial items require separate scope analysis.
Study instruction:
- Identify the contract date and distinguish a binding contractual right from a forecast or internal intention to transact.
Key point:
- Contractual participation is the recognition trigger.
- A likely future purchase or sale is not automatically a recognised financial instrument.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
34. Q: How are financial assets and liabilities measured on initial recognition?
A: Show answer
IFRS 9 generally requires initial measurement at fair value. For instruments not measured at FVPL, directly attributable transaction costs are added to the initial carrying amount of an asset or deducted from the initial carrying amount of a liability, as applicable. Transaction costs are incremental costs directly attributable to acquiring, issuing or disposing of the instrument and would not have been incurred if the transaction had not occurred. Broker, adviser and dealer fees, regulatory levies, exchange fees and transfer taxes are examples. Internal administration, holding costs, financing costs and debt premiums or discounts are not transaction costs under the definition described in the chapter. Instruments measured at FVPL do not include transaction costs in the fair-value amount in the same way; those costs are expensed.
Study instruction:
- Separate the fair-value amount from incremental transaction costs and identify which costs would not have arisen without the transaction.
Key point:
- Fair value is the starting point for initial measurement.
- Transaction-cost treatment depends on whether the instrument is measured at FVPL and whether the cost is incremental and directly attributable.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 13 Fair Value Measurement
35. Q: Why might the transaction price differ from the fair value of a financial instrument at initial recognition?
A: Show answer
The transaction price is normally the fair value of the consideration given or received. However, if part of the consideration relates to something other than the financial instrument, the entity must estimate the instrument's fair value using an appropriate valuation technique. The chapter's example is an interest-free employee loan. The nominal cash advanced is not entirely consideration for the loan because part of the benefit relates to employee services or loyalty. The loan is initially measured by discounting its future cash flows using a market rate for a comparable loan, considering currency, term and credit rating. The difference between cash advanced and the loan's fair value is accounted for separately, for example as an employee expense or a deferred employee-related amount depending on the loan's terms.
Study instruction:
- For a below-market or interest-free loan, identify any non-financial benefit and calculate the present value using a comparable market borrowing rate.
Key point:
- Transaction price is normally fair value, but bundled or concessional terms may require valuation.
- The non-financial element must be accounted for separately from the financial asset or liability.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 13 Fair Value Measurement
36. Q: What is amortised cost, and how does the effective-interest method work?
A: Show answer
Amortised cost starts with the initial carrying amount, subtracts principal repayments, adds or subtracts cumulative amortisation of any difference between the initial amount and maturity amount using the effective-interest method, and for financial assets deducts any loss allowance. The effective interest rate is the rate that discounts estimated future contractual cash receipts or payments over the expected life of the instrument to its initial gross carrying amount or amortised cost. It incorporates contractual terms, fees, transaction costs, premiums and discounts. Interest revenue or expense is allocated over the relevant periods using that rate, rather than simply applying the stated coupon to the original face value. The method therefore recognises the economic yield of the instrument over its life.
Study instruction:
- Prepare an amortised-cost schedule showing opening balance, effective-interest amount, cash coupon, principal repayment and closing balance.
Key point:
- Effective interest allocates the instrument's total yield or cost over time.
- The coupon rate and effective interest rate may differ when fees, transaction costs, premiums or discounts exist.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
37. Q: How do subsequent measurement and gain-or-loss presentation differ among the main financial-asset categories?
A: Show answer
Debt assets at amortised cost are subsequently measured using the effective-interest method and are subject to expected-credit-loss impairment. Debt assets at FVOCI are measured at fair value, with relevant cumulative fair-value changes presented in OCI, while interest and impairment effects are recognised in profit or loss; cumulative amounts are recycled to profit or loss on derecognition. Equity instruments designated at FVOCI are also measured at fair value, but gains and losses remain in OCI without recycling on disposal and no expected-credit-loss allowance is applied. Assets at FVPL are remeasured at fair value with gains and losses generally recognised in profit or loss, subject to applicable hedge-accounting and other specified exceptions. The category determines both the carrying amount and the location of performance effects.
Study instruction:
- Trace one example through initial recognition, subsequent measurement, impairment and disposal for each financial-asset category.
Key point:
- The measurement category controls where fair-value changes, interest and impairment are presented.
- Debt FVOCI and equity FVOCI must not be treated as interchangeable categories.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
38. Q: What problem did the expected-credit-loss model address, and which instruments does it cover?
A: Show answer
The incurred-loss model under IAS 39 delayed recognition until a credit-loss event occurred, making loss allowances less responsive to emerging credit deterioration during the financial crisis. IFRS 9 introduced a forward-looking expected-credit-loss model so that credit information about past events, current conditions and reasonable forecasts can influence impairment before a loss is fully realised. The chapter identifies debt instruments measured at amortised cost or FVOCI, qualifying loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts, IFRS 15 contract assets, and IFRS 16 lease receivables as items within the model. The precise scope must be checked because instruments measured at FVPL and equity investments designated at FVOCI are not subject to this impairment model.
Study instruction:
- Identify which balances in a portfolio are subject to expected-credit-loss measurement and which are excluded because of their measurement category or governing standard.
Key point:
- Expected credit losses are forward-looking rather than dependent solely on an incurred loss event.
- The impairment model applies to specified exposures, not every financial instrument.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: Post-implementation Review of IFRS 9—Impairment
39. Q: How do the three stages of the general expected-credit-loss model operate?
A: Show answer
Stage 1 applies when there has not been a significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition; the loss allowance is 12-month expected credit losses, and interest revenue is calculated on the gross carrying amount. Stage 2 applies after a significant increase in credit risk; the allowance becomes lifetime expected credit losses, while interest is still calculated on the gross carrying amount. Stage 3 applies when the financial asset is credit-impaired; lifetime expected credit losses continue to be recognised, but interest revenue is calculated on amortised cost net of the loss allowance. If credit risk later improves sufficiently, an asset can move from Stage 2 back to Stage 1. The staging decision is based on changes in the risk of default since initial recognition, not simply on the amount of collateral available.
Study instruction:
- Draw the three-stage model and show the loss horizon and interest base at each stage.
Key point:
- Stage 1 uses 12-month ECL; Stages 2 and 3 use lifetime ECL.
- Stage 3 interest is based on the net carrying amount after the loss allowance.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
40. Q: How should an entity assess whether credit risk has increased significantly?
A: Show answer
The entity compares the risk of default over the expected life of the instrument at the reporting date with the risk at initial recognition. It considers reasonable and supportable information available without undue cost or effort, including forward-looking information, external market indicators, internal factors and borrower-specific information. The assessment may be performed collectively for portfolios when risk changes are not identifiable at an individual-instrument level. Collateral affects the amount of expected loss but not the probability of default, so it is not considered when determining whether credit risk has increased significantly. The chapter notes a rebuttable presumption that a significant increase has occurred when payments are more than 30 days past due if forward-looking information is unavailable, and a low-credit-risk simplification may be available for investment-grade exposures.
Study instruction:
- Document initial and current default risk, the forward-looking indicators considered, any portfolio grouping and the reason collateral was excluded from the significant-increase assessment.
Key point:
- Compare lifetime default risk at reporting date with risk at initial recognition.
- Collateral affects loss severity, not the assessment of whether default risk has increased significantly.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
41. Q: What indicators can show that a financial asset is credit-impaired?
A: Show answer
The chapter lists indicators including significant financial difficulty of the borrower; a breach of contract or default in interest or principal payments; concessions granted because of the borrower's financial difficulty that the lender would not otherwise consider; probable bankruptcy or other financial reorganisation; disappearance of an active market because of financial difficulties; and purchase or origination at a deep discount reflecting incurred credit losses. Default is broader than a missed payment and should be consistent with the entity's internal credit-risk-management definition. The chapter notes a rebuttable presumption that default occurs no later than 90 days past due unless evidence supports a more lagging criterion. Qualitative warning signs and contractual breaches must therefore be considered alongside days-past-due data.
Study instruction:
- Build a credit-impaired checklist combining payment status, borrower financial condition, concessions, covenant breaches and market evidence.
Key point:
- Credit impairment is assessed using both qualitative and quantitative evidence.
- A 90-day past-due presumption is not a substitute for considering earlier warning indicators.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
42. Q: When can the simplified expected-credit-loss approach be used?
A: Show answer
The simplified approach avoids tracking changes in credit risk and instead recognises lifetime expected credit losses at all times. The chapter states that it must be applied to trade receivables and contract assets that do not contain a significant financing component. For trade receivables or contract assets that do contain a significant financing component, and for lease receivables, the entity may have an accounting-policy choice between the simplified and general approaches. The choice must be applied consistently, although the policy can be made independently for the relevant classes described in the chapter. The approach reduces staging complexity but does not remove the need to estimate expected losses using relevant historical, current and forward-looking information.
Study instruction:
- Classify receivables and contract assets by financing component and identify whether the simplified approach is mandatory or an accounting-policy choice.
Key point:
- The simplified approach recognises lifetime ECL throughout the exposure period.
- Policy choices must be applied consistently to the relevant classes of balances.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 16 Leases
43. Q: How are purchased or originated credit-impaired financial assets treated?
A: Show answer
The general three-stage approach does not apply to financial assets that are credit-impaired on purchase or origination. Instead of recognising a separate loss allowance at initial recognition, the expected credit losses are reflected in a credit-adjusted effective interest rate. Subsequently, changes in lifetime expected credit losses are recognised in profit or loss as impairment gains or losses. This treatment distinguishes assets acquired or originated with evidence of impairment from assets that deteriorate after initial recognition. The entity must identify the credit-impaired status at the acquisition or origination date and calculate the credit-adjusted yield using the relevant expected cash flows rather than applying the ordinary Stage 1 allowance mechanics without adjustment.
Study instruction:
- Separate purchased-or-originated credit-impaired assets from assets that become credit-impaired after recognition and identify the interest-rate basis for each.
Key point:
- Credit-impaired status at purchase or origination changes the impairment mechanics.
- Subsequent changes in lifetime ECL are recognised as impairment gains or losses.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
44. Q: What factors must be considered when measuring expected credit losses?
A: Show answer
Expected credit losses are based on the present value of cash shortfalls over the relevant exposure period. The measurement should reflect probability-weighted outcomes rather than only the most likely scenario, the time value of money, and reasonable and supportable information about past events, current conditions and forecast economic conditions. The entity generally considers the maximum contractual period over which it is exposed to credit risk, subject to specific treatment for revolving facilities. Cash shortfalls include timing differences: a loss can arise even if the entity expects full payment but expects it later than contractually due. Discounting generally uses the effective interest rate determined at initial recognition, or an appropriate approximation, with specific rules for commitments and guarantees where necessary.
Study instruction:
- Review the forecast scenarios, probability weights, expected timing of receipts, discount rate and exposure period supporting an ECL calculation.
Key point:
- ECL reflects amount, timing and probability of cash shortfalls.
- Delayed collection can create a credit loss even when the full nominal amount is eventually expected.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
45. Q: How are impairment losses presented for debt instruments at amortised cost and debt instruments at FVOCI?
A: Show answer
For debt instruments measured at amortised cost, the loss allowance is recognised as an expense in profit or loss and reduces the asset's carrying amount in the statement of financial position. For debt instruments measured at FVOCI, the impairment loss is also recognised in profit or loss, but the asset continues to be presented at fair value. The loss allowance is reflected through OCI so that the balance-sheet carrying amount remains fair value. When the asset is derecognised, cumulative amounts in OCI are recycled to profit or loss under the debt-FVOCI model. The chapter's example demonstrates that impairment accounting and fair-value movements can be presented in different places without changing the requirement to recognise the expected credit loss in profit or loss.
Study instruction:
- Reconcile the gross carrying amount, loss allowance, fair-value adjustment and OCI balance for an amortised-cost asset and an FVOCI debt asset.
Key point:
- Amortised-cost impairment reduces the asset's carrying amount directly.
- Debt-FVOCI impairment affects profit or loss while the balance-sheet asset remains at fair value.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
46. Q: When may a financial asset and financial liability be offset in the statement of financial position?
A: Show answer
IAS 32 permits offsetting only when the entity currently has a legally enforceable right to set off the recognised amounts and intends either to settle on a net basis or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously. Both conditions must be met. A commercial expectation that counterparties will settle balances together, a common supplier relationship or an internal netting spreadsheet is not sufficient by itself. The legal right normally arises from a written contract and must be enforceable in the relevant circumstances. In some arrangements involving three parties, all parties to the set-off right must be included in the legal arrangement. The conditions are deliberately strict because offsetting can affect reported liquidity and solvency measures.
Study instruction:
- For each proposed net presentation, obtain the legal agreement and document both the enforceable right and the intended settlement method.
Key point:
- A legally enforceable right and qualifying settlement intention are both required.
- Operational convenience or a matching of balances does not itself justify net presentation.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
47. Q: What is the purpose of hedge accounting under IFRS 9?
A: Show answer
Entities enter into hedges to manage exposures such as foreign-exchange, interest-rate and other price risks. Ordinary accounting may recognise gains or losses on the hedging instrument and hedged item in different periods or in different parts of the financial statements, creating accounting mismatches that do not reflect the entity's risk-management activity. Hedge accounting changes recognition or measurement so that the financial statements better reflect the economic relationship between the hedge and the exposure. IFRS 9 aims to align accounting more closely with risk management, but hedge accounting is not automatic: qualifying instruments, qualifying hedged items, formal designation and documentation, and effectiveness conditions must all be satisfied. An entity chooses whether to designate a qualifying relationship and may apply hedge accounting only from the designation date.
Study instruction:
- Identify the economic risk being managed and explain why ordinary accounting would create a timing or presentation mismatch.
Key point:
- Hedge accounting seeks to represent risk-management activity more faithfully.
- Economic hedging alone does not qualify for hedge accounting without formal designation and required criteria.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
48. Q: What makes an instrument eligible to be designated as a hedging instrument?
A: Show answer
The instrument must be designated and documented at the inception of the hedging relationship, and it must meet the IFRS 9 eligibility conditions. Derivatives are commonly used. Non-derivative financial assets or liabilities can be used only in specified circumstances, such as when they are measured at FVPL or when they hedge foreign-currency risk. Certain liabilities whose own-credit changes are presented in OCI cannot be hedging instruments, and written options generally cannot be designated by the writer except in the described relationship with a purchased option. The hedging instrument must be with a party external to the reporting entity, subject to the standard's rules. A proportion of the instrument's notional amount may be designated, but an entity cannot designate only an arbitrary portion of the period for which the instrument is outstanding.
Study instruction:
- Check instrument type, measurement category, counterparty, designation documentation and the exact proportion being designated.
Key point:
- Eligibility depends on the instrument and the documented hedge relationship.
- A risk-management contract is not automatically an eligible hedging instrument.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
49. Q: What items can qualify as a hedged item under IFRS 9?
A: Show answer
A hedged item may be a recognised asset or liability, an unrecognised firm commitment, a highly probable forecast transaction or a net investment in a foreign operation. It may be a single item, a group of items, a component of an item or, subject to conditions, a risk component of a financial or non-financial item. A firm commitment is a binding agreement to exchange a specified quantity of resources at a specified price on a specified future date; a forecast transaction is anticipated but not yet committed. The hedged item must be reliably measurable and generally arise from a transaction with a party external to the reporting entity, subject to specified exceptions. Not every exposure or management forecast is eligible.
Study instruction:
- Distinguish a binding firm commitment from a forecast transaction and document the evidence supporting the probability and measurability of the exposure.
Key point:
- IFRS 9 permits several types of recognised and future exposures to be hedged.
- Eligibility, measurability and external-party conditions must be checked.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
50. Q: What conditions must be met before hedge accounting can be applied?
A: Show answer
At inception, the entity must formally designate and document the hedging relationship, its risk-management objective and strategy, the hedging instrument, the hedged item, the nature of the risk being hedged and how effectiveness will be assessed. The relationship must contain only eligible hedging instruments and hedged items. It must also meet the effectiveness requirements: an economic relationship must exist between the hedged item and instrument; credit risk must not dominate the value changes arising from that relationship; and the hedge ratio must reflect the quantities actually hedged and used in the risk-management strategy. Documentation should be prepared when the hedge is designated, not reconstructed after gains or losses have arisen.
Study instruction:
- Assemble a hedge-designation file and test each eligibility and effectiveness condition against contemporaneous evidence.
Key point:
- Formal documentation at inception is essential.
- Effectiveness requires an economic relationship, no dominance by credit risk and an aligned hedge ratio.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
51. Q: What is the difference between a fair-value hedge and a cash-flow hedge?
A: Show answer
A fair-value hedge protects against changes in the fair value of a recognised asset, recognised liability or unrecognised firm commitment. A cash-flow hedge protects against variability in cash flows of a recognised asset or liability, or a highly probable forecast transaction. A useful distinction is that a cash-flow hedge locks in or stabilises future cash flows, whereas a fair-value hedge addresses changes in the current fair value of an existing exposure or firm commitment. A foreign-currency hedge of a firm commitment may be accounted for as either type, subject to the applicable designation and conditions. The classification determines where effective and ineffective hedge movements are recognised and when amounts accumulated in OCI are recycled or included in the cost of a non-financial item.
Study instruction:
- For each proposed hedge, state whether the risk concerns fair value today or variability in future cash flows and identify the hedged item.
Key point:
- Fair-value hedges address changes in fair value; cash-flow hedges address variability in cash flows.
- The designation affects both measurement adjustments and the timing of profit-or-loss recognition.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
52. Q: How are gains and losses accounted for in fair-value hedges and cash-flow hedges, and what should management monitor after designation?
A: Show answer
In a fair-value hedge, the hedging instrument's gain or loss is generally recognised immediately in profit or loss, and the hedged item is adjusted for the effective change in fair value attributable to the hedged risk, with the corresponding effect recognised in profit or loss. In a cash-flow hedge, the effective portion of the hedging instrument's gain or loss is recognised in OCI and the ineffective portion in profit or loss. When a forecast transaction creates a financial asset or liability, the cash-flow hedge reserve is recycled to profit or loss as the hedged cash flows affect earnings; when it creates a non-financial asset or liability, the accumulated amount is included in the initial cost or carrying amount of that item. Management must perform prospective effectiveness assessments at inception and at least each reporting date, monitor whether the risk-management objective has changed, assess whether credit risk dominates, and rebalance the hedge ratio when the relationship becomes imbalanced. If hedge accounting is discontinued, amounts in OCI are generally reclassified immediately unless the hedged future cash flows are still expected to occur, in which case they remain until those cash flows occur.
Study instruction:
- Reconcile the derivative valuation, hedged-item adjustment, OCI reserve, ineffectiveness and any basis adjustment, then document each reporting-date effectiveness assessment.
Key point:
- Fair-value hedges generally recognise offsetting fair-value effects in profit or loss; cash-flow hedges defer the effective portion in OCI.
- Ongoing monitoring, rebalancing and discontinuation decisions require evidence of the continuing economic relationship and risk-management objective.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: Post-implementation Review of IFRS 9—Hedge Accounting
53. Q: What is the purpose and scope of IFRS 7 disclosures?
A: Show answer
IFRS 7 helps users evaluate the significance of financial instruments for an entity's financial position, performance and cash flows, and the nature and extent of risks arising from those instruments. It applies broadly, including to non-financial businesses with ordinary cash, receivables and payables as well as financial institutions with complex portfolios. Its disclosure population can include recognised and certain unrecognised instruments, subject to scope exceptions. The chapter groups the requirements into information about significance, risk exposures and transferred financial assets. The disclosures should explain how instruments affect the entity and how management identifies, measures and manages the resulting risks.
Study instruction:
- "Map each financial-instrument class to the relevant IFRS 7 disclosure objective and identify the supporting register, risk report and financial-statement note."
Key point:
- IFRS 7 addresses both the significance of instruments and the risks they create.
- The requirements apply to ordinary operating entities as well as financial institutions.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
54. Q: What information does IFRS 7 require about the significance of financial instruments?
A: Show answer
Significance disclosures include carrying amounts by relevant measurement category, income and expense items, net gains and losses, and specified information about assets or liabilities designated at fair value through profit or loss and equity investments designated at FVOCI. Other disclosures address reclassifications, offsetting arrangements, collateral pledged or received, defaults and breaches, compound instruments with embedded derivatives and relevant accounting-policy choices. The purpose is to help users understand how financial instruments affect the statement of financial position and performance. Amounts and descriptions should reconcile to the underlying register and ledger and should distinguish measurement categories from disclosure classes.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare an IFRS 7 checklist and reconcile each amount and description to the instrument register, trial balance and supporting note."
Key point:
- Significance disclosures explain how instruments affect financial position and performance.
- The disclosure class is a level of aggregation for users and is not interchangeable with an IFRS 9 measurement category.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
55. Q: How should credit risk and expected credit losses be disclosed?
A: Show answer
Credit-risk disclosures should enable users to understand management's credit-risk practices, the amounts arising from expected credit losses and the entity's exposure to credit risk. Relevant information includes how significant increases in credit risk are identified, the definition of default, how credit-impaired assets are identified, the inputs and assumptions used in ECL measurement and how forward-looking information is incorporated. Quantitative information should explain changes in loss allowances and the reasons for those changes, gross exposures and significant concentrations. Collateral and other credit enhancements may also require disclosure. A useful note explains the drivers of risk and allowance movements rather than presenting only a closing provision.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile the ECL movement schedule to the general ledger and explain material transfers, additions, reversals, write-offs and changes in assumptions."
Key point:
- Credit-risk disclosure combines management practices, methodology, quantitative exposure and allowance movements.
- Users should be able to understand why the loss allowance changed and what risk remains.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: Post-implementation Review of IFRS 9—Impairment
56. Q: How should liquidity risk be disclosed under IFRS 7?
A: Show answer
Liquidity-risk disclosures include a maturity analysis of financial liabilities showing remaining contractual maturities and a description of how the entity manages the funding risk. The analysis uses contractual undiscounted cash flows, which may differ from the discounted carrying amount in the statement of financial position. Time bands should be appropriate to the entity's circumstances and the nature of its obligations. Management explanations may describe undrawn facilities, readily liquid financial assets, diversified funding sources, cash-flow forecasting and contingency funding plans. The disclosure should be consistent with information provided internally to key management personnel and should not conceal concentrations or near-term refinancing pressure.
Study instruction:
- "Rebuild the maturity analysis using contractual undiscounted payments and compare it with carrying amounts and treasury liquidity forecasts."
Key point:
- The maturity analysis uses contractual undiscounted cash flows.
- Users also need to understand how management plans to meet obligations as they fall due.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
57. Q: How should market risk sensitivity analysis be prepared and explained?
A: Show answer
Market-risk sensitivity analysis shows how profit or loss and equity would have been affected by reasonably possible changes in relevant risk variables at the reporting date. The principal categories are currency risk, interest-rate risk and other price risk. The entity should disclose the methods and assumptions used and explain material changes from the previous period. For example, a variable-rate liability may require analysis of how reasonably possible interest-rate changes would affect interest expense. If management uses a model that captures interdependencies among risk variables, the disclosure should explain that method rather than presenting isolated sensitivities that misrepresent the exposure. The analysis should be consistent with actual positions and internal risk information.
Study instruction:
- "Select reasonably possible shocks for each material market risk and reconcile the sensitivity model to the reporting-date positions."
Key point:
- Sensitivity analysis quantifies how market variables could affect profit or loss and equity.
- Methods, assumptions and changes must be transparent enough for users to interpret the results.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
58. Q: What disclosures are required for financial assets transferred to another entity?
A: Show answer
IFRS 7 requires information about transferred financial assets that have not been derecognised in their entirety and assets derecognised while the transferor retains continuing involvement. The disclosures help users understand the relationship between transferred assets and associated liabilities and assess the nature and risks of continuing involvement. Information may include the nature of the assets transferred, risks and rewards retained, the relationship with associated liabilities and quantitative details about continuing involvement. This is relevant to factoring, securitisation, repurchase arrangements and other structures where legal transfer does not necessarily remove all exposure from the transferor.
Study instruction:
- "Review a receivables sale or securitisation agreement and map the transferred assets, associated liabilities, retained rights and continuing obligations."
Key point:
- Legal transfer does not automatically mean all accounting exposure has ended.
- Continuing involvement and retained risks must be disclosed when the IFRS 7 criteria apply.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
59. Q: How do collateral, defaults, breaches and netting arrangements affect financial-instrument disclosures?
A: Show answer
IFRS 7 requires specified information about collateral pledged and, in relevant circumstances, collateral received that the entity may sell or repledge. Defaults and breaches on loans payable may require disclosure of the event, the carrying amount of affected loans and whether the default was remedied before the financial statements were authorised. Netting disclosures help users understand the effects of offsetting and enforceable master netting arrangements, even when the balance sheet does not present the instruments net. These notes should be supported by executed agreements, collateral registers, covenant-monitoring records and legal assessments. Collateral does not eliminate credit risk, and disclosure of a netting arrangement does not by itself satisfy IAS 32's offsetting criteria.
Study instruction:
- "Tie collateral, default and netting disclosures to loan agreements, covenant reports, security registers and legal confirmations."
Key point:
- These disclosures explain risk mitigation, contractual breaches and enforceable arrangements.
- A disclosed netting arrangement does not automatically permit balance-sheet offsetting.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation
60. Q: What should an entity disclose about hedge accounting and its risk-management strategy?
A: Show answer
Hedge disclosures should explain the entity's risk-management strategy, how it applies that strategy to each risk category, which instruments are used, how the economic relationship is assessed and how risk components are determined. Users should understand the terms of the hedging instruments, how hedging activity affects the amount, timing and uncertainty of future cash flows, and the effect of hedge accounting on financial position and performance. Tabular information may be required for carrying amounts, presentation, fair-value changes, notional amounts and hedge ineffectiveness, separated by risk category and hedge type. The disclosure should agree with treasury documentation, derivative valuations and reserve movements.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile the hedge register to derivative valuations, reserve movements, ineffectiveness calculations and the financial-risk narrative."
Key point:
- Hedge disclosures connect accounting results with the entity's actual risk-management strategy.
- Quantitative tables and qualitative explanations should tell a consistent story about exposures and cash flows.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: Post-implementation Review of IFRS 9—Hedge Accounting
61. Q: How should fair-value information for financial instruments be presented?
A: Show answer
IFRS 7 requires fair-value information for each relevant class of financial assets and liabilities in a way that permits comparison with carrying amounts, subject to specified requirements and exemptions. IFRS 13 supplies the fair-value measurement framework: fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. The entity should use appropriate valuation techniques and inputs, consider market activity and liquidity, and disclose significant methods and inputs where required. A quoted price, model output or management estimate does not remove the need to assess whether the measurement reflects the applicable market-participant objective.
Study instruction:
- "For each instrument class, compare carrying amount with fair value and document the valuation technique, significant inputs and hierarchy disclosures."
Key point:
- IFRS 13 governs measurement; IFRS 7 provides related financial-instrument disclosures.
- Fair value is a market-participant exit price at the measurement date, not an entity-specific target value.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 13 Fair Value Measurement
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
62. Q: What did the IASB conclude in its post-implementation review of IFRS 9 impairment?
A: Show answer
In July 2024 the IASB concluded that IFRS 9's impairment requirements were working as intended. The review found that the expected-credit-loss model had led to more timely recognition of credit losses than the former IAS 39 incurred-loss model and provided useful information to investors. The IASB nevertheless identified targeted areas for improvement, particularly some credit-risk disclosure requirements and application questions requiring clarification. This conclusion is not a guarantee that every entity's ECL estimate is accurate; entities still need sound data, reasonable forecasts, appropriate staging and transparent assumptions. The review provides useful context for evaluating the standard's overall design and implementation.
Study instruction:
- "Read the IASB's review summary and distinguish its overall conclusion from the targeted application and disclosure matters it identified."
Key point:
- The IASB concluded that the IFRS 9 impairment model was working as intended and improved timeliness.
- The review still identified targeted opportunities to improve credit-risk disclosures and application guidance.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: Post-implementation Review of IFRS 9—Impairment
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
63. Q: What is the current status of the IASB's post-implementation review of IFRS 9 hedge accounting?
A: Show answer
As of 24 November 2026, the IASB had completed Phase 1 outreach and published its Request for Information on 28 September 2026 for the post-implementation review of IFRS 9 hedge accounting and related IFRS 7 disclosures. The comment period is scheduled to close on 26 January 2027. The review assesses whether the requirements are working as intended for users, preparers, auditors and regulators. It does not itself change the existing accounting requirements. Preparers should continue applying the current standards while monitoring the review and any later standard-setting decisions.
Study instruction:
- "Check the IFRS Foundation project page for the current consultation status and distinguish a post-implementation review from an issued amendment."
Key point:
- The review is evaluating how hedge-accounting and related disclosure requirements operate in practice.
- A consultation or review does not change the applicable accounting requirements until formal amendments are issued and become effective.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: Post-implementation Review of IFRS 9—Hedge Accounting
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
64. Q: What empirical evidence discussed in the chapter suggests about market reactions to expected-credit-loss accounting?
A: Show answer
The chapter's academic perspective reports research by Onali and co-authors finding a positive market reaction around adoption events for the expected-loss model in IFRS 9, with results consistent with investors valuing more timely information and stronger monitoring. This is evidence about investor response in the study's sample and research design; it does not prove that every ECL estimate is unbiased or that implementation costs are immaterial. The IASB's later post-implementation review separately concluded that the impairment requirements were working as intended and had improved timeliness. The two forms of evidence should be kept distinct: one is an empirical market study, the other is the standard-setter's review.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the study's sample and market-reaction finding with the IASB's post-implementation review, and avoid treating association as proof of causation."
Key point:
- Research can inform how investors respond to ECL information.
- Market-reaction evidence and the IASB's standard review answer different questions and should not be conflated.
Source links:
- Onali et al. (2024): Market Reaction to the Expected Loss Model in Banks
- IFRS Foundation: Post-implementation Review of IFRS 9—Impairment
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
65. Q: What does research on loan-loss allowances suggest about the information content of impairment charges?
A: Show answer
The chapter discusses Beaver and Engel's research on the market pricing of discretionary and non-discretionary components of bank loan-loss allowances. The study suggests that investors may interpret the components differently: a non-discretionary component reflects underlying asset impairment, while a discretionary component may contain additional information when it signals management's assessment or response. This does not permit management to use provisions as a signalling device. IFRS 9 still requires expected credit losses to be measured using unbiased, probability-weighted and supportable information. The research is useful for understanding why allowance disclosures and transparent assumptions matter to investors.
Study instruction:
- "Separate the economic credit deterioration from management's estimation choices and assess whether the allowance assumptions are supportable."
Key point:
- Loan-loss allowances can convey information about both exposures and management's assessment.
- Empirical findings do not override the measurement requirements or justify discretionary provisioning.
Source links:
- Beaver and Engel (1996): Loan-loss Allowances and Security Prices
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
66. Q: How can financial-statement classification of hybrid instruments affect investor judgments?
A: Show answer
The chapter summarises research by Patrick Hopkins showing that the balance-sheet classification of hybrid instruments can influence financial analysts' stock-price judgments. The result illustrates that classification is not merely a technical presentation choice: users may interpret a liability differently from an equity instrument when assessing leverage, financing risk and valuation. This effect helps explain why issuers may have incentives to structure instruments for a preferred presentation. However, the accounting outcome remains governed by IAS 32's contractual tests, not by the market reaction management wants to produce. Analysts should also distinguish accounting equity from covenant definitions and regulatory capital.
Study instruction:
- "Review a hybrid instrument from the perspectives of the issuer, investor and lender, then identify which contractual features determine its IAS 32 classification."
Key point:
- Presentation can influence user judgments and financing behaviour.
- The accounting classification must still follow contractual substance and the IAS 32 criteria.
Source links:
- Hopkins (1996): Classification of Hybrid Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation
67. Q: How does research on hedge accounting relate to corporate risk management and transparency?
A: Show answer
The chapter discusses research indicating that hedge-accounting rules can influence whether entities undertake economically useful hedging and how clearly investors understand risk management. Panaretou, Shackleton and Taylor examine the relationship between corporate risk management and hedge accounting, while the chapter notes that disclosure and more transparent reporting can improve the information environment. At the same time, restrictive qualifying criteria may discourage some economically sensible hedges from receiving hedge-accounting treatment. The practical implication is to distinguish the economic hedge from its accounting designation and to explain any resulting mismatch clearly. Current IASB review work is examining how the IFRS 9 hedge-accounting requirements operate in practice.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the economic purpose of a hedge with the formal accounting designation and identify what the entity should disclose when the two do not align."
Key point:
- Hedge-accounting rules can affect both risk-management incentives and the information users receive.
- An economic hedge does not automatically qualify for hedge accounting; eligibility and documentation remain necessary.
Source links:
- Panaretou, Shackleton and Taylor (2013): Corporate Risk Management and Hedge Accounting
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
68. Q: Why does securitisation require careful analysis of retained interests and valuation assumptions?
A: Show answer
Securitisation may transfer receivables while the originator retains servicing rights, subordinated interests, guarantees or other continuing involvement. Derecognition depends on the applicable transfer, risk-and-reward and control requirements, not merely on legal sale. The chapter's academic perspective discusses evidence that managers may have incentives to influence fair-value gains on retained cash-flow streams through discount-rate and other valuation assumptions. Research by Barth and co-authors also examines how retained interests relate to securitising firms' credit risk. The entity should document transferred rights, retained cash flows, recourse, valuation inputs and continuing involvement, and provide the IFRS 7 disclosures required.
Study instruction:
- "Map the securitisation cash flows retained by the originator and independently challenge discount rates, default assumptions and continuing-involvement conclusions."
Key point:
- Securitisation does not automatically remove all financial risk or justify derecognition.
- Retained interests and valuation assumptions can materially affect reported gains and risk disclosures.
Source links:
- Barth, Ormazabal and Taylor (2012): Asset Securitizations and Credit Risk
- Dechow, Myers and Shakespeare (2010): Fair Value Accounting and Securitisation Gains
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 13 Fair Value Measurement
69. Q: What controls should exist over a financial-instrument register and classification process?
A: Show answer
A controlled register should capture instrument identity, counterparty, contract date, principal or notional amount, currency, maturity, coupon, embedded features, classification, measurement category, fair-value source, effective interest rate, impairment stage, collateral, hedge designation and disclosure class. Finance should reconcile the register to the general ledger, bank confirmations, broker statements and treasury records. Legal or technical specialists should review complex terms, while independent reviewers approve significant classification and valuation judgments. Contract amendments, business-model changes, credit deterioration and changes in hedge relationships should trigger reassessment. The register should retain source documents and an audit trail of decisions.
Study instruction:
- "Design a register with required fields, owner, reviewer, source-document reference, change log and periodic reconciliation status."
Key point:
- A complete register supports classification, measurement, impairment, hedging and disclosure together.
- Reconciliation and change-trigger controls reduce omissions and inconsistent treatment.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
70. Q: How can period-end review detect financial-instrument accounting errors and omissions?
A: Show answer
Period-end review should compare the contract inventory with ledger balances, bank and broker confirmations, treasury reports, valuation files, interest schedules, ECL models and hedge documentation. Reviewers should investigate missing instruments, stale fair values, unrecorded fees, incorrect effective-interest calculations, unexpected ECL stage transfers, unrecognised derivatives, covenant breaches and mismatches between OCI reserves and supporting schedules. The review should also confirm that disclosure tables reconcile to the underlying data and that significant judgments are supported by current evidence. A strong close process tests both recorded balances and omitted contractual exposures.
Study instruction:
- "Create a month-end checklist that reconciles instruments to external confirmations and tests fair value, effective interest, ECL, hedge accounting and disclosure schedules."
Key point:
- A complete close process tests recorded balances and omitted contractual exposures.
- Exceptions should be assigned, evidenced, corrected and closed before financial statements are authorised.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
71. Q: What recent IFRS amendments should preparers consider when applying IFRS 9 and IFRS 7?
A: Show answer
The IASB issued amendments to IFRS 9 and IFRS 7 in May 2024 addressing matters including financial liabilities settled using electronic payment systems, the assessment of contractual cash-flow characteristics of financial assets and related disclosures. The chapter's core framework remains useful, but preparers should not rely solely on an older textbook description when applying current requirements. They should check the issued amendment, its effective date, transition provisions and any entity-specific early-adoption decision. The appropriate accounting conclusion depends on the reporting period and the authoritative text in force for that period.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the chapter's description with the current IFRS Foundation amendment page and record the effective date and transition provisions relevant to the reporting entity."
Key point:
- Standards evolve, and later amendments can refine classification, measurement and disclosure.
- Always confirm the version and effective date applicable to the reporting period.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: 2024 Amendments to Classification and Measurement of Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures
72. Q: What are the most important practical lessons for preparing financial statements with financial instruments?
A: Show answer
A reliable process begins with complete contract identification and classification under IAS 32 and IFRS 9. It then applies the correct initial and subsequent measurement, calculates effective interest and ECL where relevant, evaluates derivatives and embedded features, assesses offsetting and hedge accounting, and prepares IFRS 7 disclosures. The entity should maintain a controlled register, reconcile to external confirmations and the general ledger, document valuation and credit assumptions, monitor changes in business models and contracts, and obtain independent review of significant judgments. Financial-instrument reporting is a connected process: a mistake in scope or classification can affect measurement, profit or loss, OCI, ratios and disclosures at the same time.
Study instruction:
- "Use the standards map to walk one instrument from contract review through journal entries, impairment, risk management and disclosure."
Key point:
- Correct financial-instrument reporting requires an integrated lifecycle process.
- Complete contracts, documented judgment and reconciled disclosures are the foundation of reliable reporting.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments
- IFRS Foundation: IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures

Table 14
IFRS 2: Share-Based Payment Recognition, Measurement, and Disclosure
1. Q: What is the objective of IFRS 2 Share-based Payment, and why does the standard require recognition of these arrangements?
A: Show answer
IFRS 2 requires an entity to recognise goods or services received or acquired in a share-based payment arrangement and the corresponding effect on equity or liabilities. The standard treats the arrangement as an economic exchange even when the entity does not pay cash. Recognising the transaction makes the cost of employee services, professional services, inventory or other goods visible in the financial statements and improves the relevance and comparability of reported performance. The accounting entry depends on the settlement form, but the receipt of goods or services is not ignored merely because the consideration is shares, options or a share-price-linked cash amount.
Study instruction:
- "Explain why an equity award can create an accounting cost even though the entity does not make an immediate cash payment."
Key point:
- A share-based arrangement is an economic transaction that must be reflected in the financial statements.
- The form of settlement determines whether the corresponding credit is equity or a liability.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
2. Q: What is a share-based payment transaction under IFRS 2, and what kinds of goods or services can it cover?
A: Show answer
A share-based payment is an arrangement in which an entity receives or acquires goods or services as consideration for its own equity instruments, or incurs an obligation to transfer cash or other assets for amounts based on the price or value of those instruments. Goods can include inventory, consumables, property, plant and equipment, intangible assets and other non-financial assets. Services commonly include employee labour and professional services. The arrangement can involve employees or other suppliers. The key question is whether the goods or services are exchanged under terms linked to the entity's equity instruments, not whether the counterparty is an employee.
Study instruction:
- "Classify three real or hypothetical arrangements and identify the goods or services received and the equity-price link."
Key point:
- IFRS 2 covers more than employee share options; it can apply to goods and services supplied by other parties.
- Identify the substance of the arrangement before deciding on the accounting.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
3. Q: What are the three principal forms of share-based payment covered by IFRS 2?
A: Show answer
The chapter distinguishes equity-settled transactions, cash-settled transactions and arrangements in which the entity or counterparty has a choice of settlement. In an equity-settled transaction, goods or services are received in exchange for the entity's own equity instruments. In a cash-settled transaction, the entity incurs a liability to pay cash or other assets by reference to the value of its equity instruments. A choice arrangement may contain both a debt component and an equity component, or its classification may depend on whether the entity has a present obligation to pay cash. The classification drives measurement and subsequent remeasurement.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a comparison table showing the settlement right, initial credit and subsequent measurement for each form."
Key point:
- Equity-settled normally creates an equity credit; cash-settled creates a remeasured liability.
- A settlement choice requires analysis of whose choice it is and whether a cash obligation exists.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
4. Q: How does IFRS 2 apply when one entity in a group receives services but another group entity settles the award?
A: Show answer
The chapter explains that the standard applies to group arrangements in which an entity receives goods or services but another entity in the same group, or a shareholder of that other entity, is required to settle the share-based payment. It also applies when one group entity must settle an award for goods or services received by another group entity. The receiving entity should identify which entity obtained the employee or supplier services and which entity has the settlement obligation. The group relationship does not remove the need to recognise the transaction. The detailed entries in separate financial statements should be determined under the applicable IFRS 2 group-arrangement requirements.
Study instruction:
- "Map the service recipient, legal employer, award-granting entity and settling entity for a group-based incentive plan."
Key point:
- Group structure does not by itself take an arrangement outside IFRS 2.
- Document both the entity receiving the goods or services and the entity responsible for settlement.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
5. Q: Which business-combination transactions are excluded from IFRS 2, and which later plan changes may remain within its scope?
A: Show answer
Equity instruments issued in a business combination in exchange for obtaining control of the acquiree are excluded from IFRS 2 and are accounted for under IFRS 3. The chapter distinguishes that acquisition consideration from changes to an existing share-based payment plan. Cancellation, replacement or modification of an existing plan arising because of a business combination or restructuring can remain subject to IFRS 2. The accountant therefore needs to determine whether the instruments are consideration for obtaining control or whether the transaction changes an award that already exists. The legal documents and acquisition terms should be reviewed rather than classifying every award issued around an acquisition in the same way.
Study instruction:
- "For an acquisition-related award, identify whether it is consideration for control or a change to an existing employee award."
Key point:
- Equity instruments issued as business-combination consideration are dealt with under IFRS 3.
- Changes to pre-existing share-based payment plans may still require IFRS 2 accounting.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
6. Q: Why is a transaction with an employee acting solely in the capacity of an equity holder generally outside IFRS 2?
A: Show answer
IFRS 2 does not treat every transfer of shares to an employee as remuneration. The chapter explains that a transaction with an employee who holds equity instruments in the employing entity in the capacity of an equity holder is outside the standard. A rights issue offered to existing shareholders on favourable terms is an example: the employee participates because of shareholder status, not because services are being received. The accountant must distinguish an employee award for work from a transaction made on the same basis as other shareholders. The substance, eligibility criteria and purpose of the arrangement are important evidence.
Study instruction:
- "Compare an employee share-option award for services with a pro-rata rights issue offered to all shareholders."
Key point:
- The employee's capacity in the transaction matters.
- A shareholder transaction is not automatically employee compensation.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
7. Q: When must an entity recognise goods or services received in a share-based payment transaction?
A: Show answer
Under the recognition principle described in IFRS 2 paragraph 7, goods or services are recognised when the entity receives them. The corresponding credit is an increase in equity for an equity-settled transaction or an increase in a liability for a cash-settled transaction. Recognition is linked to receipt of the goods or performance of the service, rather than simply to the date on which cash is paid or the award is eventually exercised. Where services are provided over a vesting period, the expense or qualifying asset is recognised as the service is rendered. The entity should align award records with payroll, procurement and period-end cut-off procedures.
Study instruction:
- "Trace a service award from grant through service delivery and identify the reporting periods in which services are received."
Key point:
- Recognition follows receipt of goods or services.
- The settlement form determines the corresponding equity or liability entry.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
8. Q: When should the debit in a share-based payment be recognised as an asset rather than an expense?
A: Show answer
The debit follows the normal recognition requirements of the relevant asset standard. If the goods received qualify as an asset, the entity recognises that asset and the corresponding equity or liability; the expense arises later when the asset is consumed, sold, depreciated or otherwise expensed under the applicable standard. Services are usually consumed as they are received, so an expense is commonly recognised as the service is rendered. Goods obtained for research activities may fail the asset-recognition criteria even if they have not physically been consumed, in which case they are expensed. Share-based consideration does not create an exemption from the normal asset-recognition tests.
Study instruction:
- "For an award exchanged for inventory, equipment and research services, determine whether each debit qualifies as an asset under the relevant standard."
Key point:
- Share-based payment determines the consideration accounting, not whether an item qualifies as an asset.
- Apply the relevant asset-recognition criteria before recording an asset.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
9. Q: What are the basic journal-entry patterns for equity-settled and cash-settled share-based payments?
A: Show answer
For an equity-settled award, the entity debits an appropriate asset or expense and credits equity as the goods or services are received. For a cash-settled award, it debits the asset or expense and credits a liability. For example, if employee services of 100,000 currency units are received under an equity-settled award, the basic entry is Dr employee expense 100,000 and Cr equity reserve 100,000, subject to the vesting-period calculation. If the same service is cash-settled, the credit is a share-based payment liability. The amounts must follow the applicable measurement rules, not an assumed cash price.
Study instruction:
- "Write both journal entries for the same service arrangement and explain why only the cash-settled liability is subsequently remeasured."
Key point:
- Equity-settled: debit asset or expense and credit equity.
- Cash-settled: debit asset or expense and credit liability.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
10. Q: How is an equity-settled transaction measured when the fair value of the goods or services can be estimated reliably?
A: Show answer
The chapter states that goods or services received in an equity-settled transaction are measured at their fair value unless that fair value cannot be estimated reliably. For parties other than employees, IFRS 2 contains a rebuttable presumption that the fair value of goods or services can be measured reliably. When direct measurement is reliable, the entity uses the fair value of what it receives and recognises the corresponding increase in equity. The measurement date is linked to the receipt of goods or performance of services for these non-employee transactions. Evidence such as observable market prices, supplier quotations or comparable service rates may support the estimate.
Study instruction:
- "Identify the observable evidence that could support a direct fair-value estimate for professional services received in exchange for shares."
Key point:
- Direct fair value of goods or services is the normal measurement basis when it is reliable.
- The presumption of reliable measurement for non-employee transactions can be rebutted only with support.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
11. Q: Why are employee services in equity-settled share-based payment arrangements normally measured by reference to the equity instruments granted?
A: Show answer
The fair value of employee services is generally considered difficult to estimate reliably because the service is not ordinarily traded as a separate market transaction. IFRS 2 therefore measures the employee services indirectly by reference to the fair value of the equity instruments granted. For employee awards, that fair value is measured at grant date. The resulting amount is recognised over the vesting period when the employee must provide future service, or immediately when the award vests at once. This approach provides a consistent measurement basis even though the entity cannot directly observe a market price for the employee's particular services.
Study instruction:
- "Explain why the fair value of an employee's services is usually not measured using the employee's salary or an external consultant's hourly rate."
Key point:
- Employee service fair value is normally measured indirectly through the equity instrument.
- For employee equity-settled awards, grant-date fair value is the key measurement basis.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
12. Q: What is the significance of grant date in measuring an employee equity-settled award?
A: Show answer
Grant date is the measurement date for the fair value of equity instruments granted to employees under the approach described in the chapter. Once the grant-date fair value is established, it is used to measure the employee services over the vesting period, subject to adjustments for relevant vesting conditions such as service and non-market performance conditions. Unlike a cash-settled liability, the equity-settled employee award is not remeasured at each reporting date merely because the share price changes. Market conditions are reflected in the grant-date fair value rather than subsequently being used to reverse the recognised amount when the employee satisfies the other vesting conditions.
Study instruction:
- "Separate grant date, service period, vesting date and exercise date on a timeline for an employee option plan."
Key point:
- Grant-date fair value anchors measurement of employee equity-settled awards.
- Do not apply cash-settled remeasurement to an equity-settled award.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
13. Q: What does vesting mean under IFRS 2?
A: Show answer
An entitlement vests when the counterparty's right to receive cash, other assets or equity instruments is no longer conditional on satisfying vesting conditions. Before vesting, the employee or supplier must still meet the conditions specified in the award, such as remaining in employment for a defined period or achieving a performance target. Vesting is not the same as exercising an option: an option may vest and become exercisable while the holder chooses not to exercise it. The distinction is essential because it determines the period over which services are recognised and whether the entity adjusts the number of instruments expected to vest.
Study instruction:
- "Use a sample option plan to distinguish grant, vesting, exercisability, exercise and expiry dates."
Key point:
- Vesting occurs when the relevant vesting conditions have been satisfied.
- Vesting and exercise are different events.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
14. Q: How is an equity-settled award accounted for when it vests immediately?
A: Show answer
If the equity instruments vest immediately, the counterparty is not required to complete a specified future service period before becoming unconditionally entitled to the instruments. The chapter explains that the services received are recognised in full on grant date, with a corresponding increase in equity. There is no future vesting period over which to spread the expense. The entity should nevertheless confirm that no substantive vesting condition remains and that the employee has received the service or other consideration required by the arrangement. Documentation should support the grant terms and the conclusion that vesting is immediate.
Study instruction:
- "Review an award agreement and determine whether the employee has to provide future service after grant date."
Key point:
- Immediate vesting generally means immediate recognition of the services received.
- Do not defer an expense over a service period that does not exist.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
15. Q: How should an equity-settled employee award be recognised when the employee must complete a service period before vesting?
A: Show answer
When an award does not vest until the employee completes a specified period of service, the entity recognises the services and corresponding increase in equity over that vesting period as the services are rendered. At each reporting date, the cumulative expense is based on the grant-date fair value, the number of instruments expected to vest and the portion of the service period completed. The expense for the current period is the updated cumulative amount less the amount already recognised. This cumulative catch-up method ensures that the final recognised amount reflects the services received and the instruments that ultimately vest.
Study instruction:
- "Build a vesting-period schedule showing grant-date fair value, expected instruments, elapsed service and cumulative expense at each reporting date."
Key point:
- Recognise employee services over the period in which the employee earns the award.
- Current-period expense is the revised cumulative amount less prior recognised expense.
Source links:
- IFRS 2 Standard (IFRS Foundation)
- KPMG: IFRS 2 Share-based Payments Handbook
16. Q: How should expected employee departures affect the number of equity instruments included in an equity-settled expense calculation?
A: Show answer
