Similar matching applies to foreign-operation translation and other items recognised outside profit or loss. Identify the original statement location so reversals are presented consistently.
Study instruction:
- "Calculate the tax effect of an upward revaluation and record the deferred tax and net surplus in OCI."
Key point:
- Tax on an OCI item is recognised in OCI.
- The tax effect is recorded with the same reserve as the underlying item.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
44. Q: How is deferred tax accounted for in a business combination?
A: Show answer
Deferred tax on identifiable acquired assets and liabilities is generally recognised when IAS 12 criteria are met. It affects acquisition accounting because it changes identifiable net assets and therefore goodwill or a bargain-purchase gain. An acquiree's previously unrecognised DTA may become recognisable after acquisition if the acquirer can demonstrate probable future taxable profit. Acquisition-date recognition must be distinguished from later changes in estimates.
Study instruction:
- "Trace an acquired asset's fair-value adjustment to tax base, deferred tax and goodwill."
Key point:
- Acquisition-date deferred tax affects identifiable net assets and goodwill.
- Later recognition of an acquired DTA may have a different accounting location.
Source links:
- IFRS 3 Business Combinations
45. Q: How are current and deferred tax balances presented?
A: Show answer
Current tax assets and liabilities are presented separately from deferred tax assets and liabilities, subject to permitted offsetting. IAS 1 governs overall presentation and current/non-current classification; deferred tax assets and liabilities are not classified as current. Tax relating to profit or loss is presented there, while tax relating to OCI or equity is presented with the underlying item.
Study instruction:
- "Review the statement of financial position and profit or loss for separate current and deferred tax presentation."
Key point:
- Current tax and deferred tax are distinct balances.
- Deferred tax balances are non-current under IAS 1 presentation.
Source links:
- IAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements
46. Q: When may current tax assets and liabilities be offset?
A: Show answer
Offsetting requires a legally enforceable right to set off recognised amounts and an intention either to settle net or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously. A common tax authority or operational netting practice alone is insufficient. If either condition is absent, present balances gross.
Study instruction:
- "Obtain legal evidence for a proposed current-tax offset and document settlement intention."
Key point:
- Legal enforceability and qualifying settlement intention are both required.
- A common tax authority alone does not permit offsetting.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
47. Q: When may deferred tax assets and liabilities be offset?
A: Show answer
Offsetting requires a legally enforceable right to offset current tax and that deferred balances relate to income taxes levied by the same authority on the same taxable entity. Different entities may offset only when they intend net or simultaneous settlement in each future period in which significant deferred amounts reverse. The test is stricter than simply operating in one country or tax group.
Study instruction:
- "Map deferred tax balances by entity and authority and assess the legal right and future settlement arrangement."
Key point:
- Deferred tax offsetting requires a current-tax set-off right and specified entity and authority conditions.
- Different taxable entities must meet additional settlement conditions.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
48. Q: What are the major components of income tax expense disclosed under IAS 12?
A: Show answer
The note explains major components such as current tax expense, prior-period adjustments, deferred tax from temporary differences, tax-rate changes, benefits from previously unrecognised losses and tax effects recognised in OCI or equity. Components reconcile to total tax expense. This helps users understand whether tax expense is driven by current taxable profit, temporary differences, changes in law or one-off items.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a tax-expense note separating current tax, deferred tax, rate changes and material other components."
Key point:
- IAS 12 requires disclosure of major tax-expense components.
- The note should reconcile to total tax recognised.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
49. Q: How does the tax-rate reconciliation help users?
A: Show answer
The reconciliation compares expected tax based on accounting profit and the applicable rate with actual tax expense. Differences may arise from non-deductible expenses, non-taxable income, foreign rates, incentives, losses, prior-period adjustments and deferred tax movements. An entity may reconcile tax expense or effective tax rate and must explain the basis for the applicable rate. This helps users assess the causes and sustainability of the rate.
Study instruction:
- "Reperform the reconciliation and explain each material reconciling item."
Key point:
- The reconciliation explains why actual tax differs from tax at the applicable rate.
- Permanent differences and jurisdictional rate effects are common reconciling items.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
50. Q: What deferred tax information is disclosed by type of temporary difference?
A: Show answer
IAS 12 requires information about recognised DTAs and DTLs for each type of temporary difference and relevant unused losses and credits. Disclose amounts recognised for each period and, where not otherwise apparent, deferred tax income or expense in profit or loss. A movement analysis may be needed for depreciation, employee benefits, receivables and provisions. The note should reconcile to closing balances and explain significant changes.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a deferred-tax note by category and reconcile opening balances, movements and closing balances."
Key point:
- Disclosures show the nature and amount of material temporary differences.
- Users need to understand closing balances and material movements.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
51. Q: What must be disclosed about unrecognised deferred tax assets?
A: Show answer
Disclose deductible temporary differences, unused losses and credits for which no DTA is recognised, with expiry information where applicable. If a DTA is recognised despite recent losses, disclose the amount and nature of evidence supporting recognition. These disclosures distinguish legal tax benefits from benefits meeting the accounting recognition criteria and show sensitivity to future profitability.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile the tax-loss register to unrecognised amounts, expiry dates and evidence for recognised assets."
Key point:
- Unrecognised tax benefits may be material even when absent from the balance sheet.
- Loss-related DTA recognition may require disclosure of supporting evidence.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
52. Q: What is disclosed about deferred tax liabilities on investments?
A: Show answer
IAS 12 requires disclosure of aggregate temporary differences associated with investments in subsidiaries, branches, associates and joint arrangements for which DTLs have not been recognised. Explain why the exception applies, including control over reversal timing and the expectation that differences will not reverse in the foreseeable future. Distribution plans, disposal intentions and legal restrictions support the assessment.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare an investment-tax schedule showing temporary differences and the non-recognition rationale."
Key point:
- Unrecognised investment-related DTLs require disclosure of aggregate differences.
- The control and foreseeable-reversal assessment should be documented.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
53. Q: When are tax consequences of dividends or distributions disclosed?
A: Show answer
Where tax rates differ depending on whether profits are distributed, IAS 12 requires disclosure of the nature and amounts of potential income-tax consequences of dividends, to the extent practicable. This helps users understand possible withholding or other taxes on distributions. The requirement applies where the jurisdiction's tax structure makes distributions relevant under the Standard.
Study instruction:
- "Check whether tax rates differ for distributed and undistributed profits and document potential consequences."
Key point:
- Distribution-related tax disclosure depends on jurisdictional tax rules.
- Material potential tax consequences of dividends should be explained where required.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
54. Q: What is IFRIC 23 and how does it complement IAS 12?
A: Show answer
IFRIC 23 explains how to reflect uncertainty over income-tax treatments when it is unclear whether a tax authority will accept a position used or planned in a filing. IAS 12 provides general recognition and measurement requirements but not the full method for uncertain treatments. IFRIC 23 requires an entity to assess whether acceptance is probable and, when it is not, reflect uncertainty in taxable profit, tax bases, unused losses and credits and tax rates.
Study instruction:
- "Identify an uncertain tax treatment and explain why IFRIC 23 is needed in addition to IAS 12."
Key point:
- IFRIC 23 adds requirements for uncertain tax treatments.
- It operates through IAS 12 current and deferred tax calculations.
Source links:
- IFRIC 23 Uncertainty over Income Tax Treatments
55. Q: How does IFRIC 23 measure an uncertain tax treatment?
A: Show answer
Assume the tax authority will examine reported amounts and know all relevant information. Assess whether acceptance is probable. If it is, use the treatment in the filing; if not, reflect uncertainty using the most likely amount or expected value, whichever better predicts resolution. Apply the method consistently and reassess when facts change. The uncertainty may affect both current and deferred tax.
Study instruction:
- "Apply IFRIC 23 to a disputed deduction and compare the two measurement methods."
Key point:
- Assume full examination and knowledge by the tax authority.
- Use the method that best predicts resolution when acceptance is not probable.
Source links:
- IFRIC 23 Uncertainty over Income Tax Treatments
56. Q: How did the 2021 single-transaction amendment affect deferred tax on leases?
A: Show answer
The amendment narrowed the initial-recognition exemption so it no longer applies to transactions that initially create equal taxable and deductible temporary differences. This matters for leases and decommissioning obligations where an asset and liability are recognised together. The entity generally recognises related DTA and DTL, subject to DTA recoverability and offsetting. The amendment is effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023, with early application permitted.
Study instruction:
- "For a lease commencement, calculate temporary differences on the right-of-use asset and lease liability."
Key point:
- The initial-recognition exemption is narrower after the 2021 amendment.
- Single transactions creating equal taxable and deductible differences generally require deferred tax.
Source links:
- 2021 IAS 12 Single-Transaction Amendment
57. Q: What is the temporary exception for Pillar Two deferred tax?
A: Show answer
The 2023 IAS 12 amendments introduced a mandatory temporary exception from recognising and disclosing deferred tax assets and liabilities related to Pillar Two income taxes. An entity discloses that it has applied the exception and continues targeted disclosures for affected entities. The exception does not remove current-tax recognition once Pillar Two tax becomes payable. Entities should monitor legislation in each jurisdiction and current IAS 12 requirements.
Study instruction:
- "Assess whether the group is within Pillar Two legislation and document the exception and current-tax process."
Key point:
- Pillar Two has a specific temporary deferred-tax exception.
- The exception does not remove current tax recognition or targeted disclosures.
Source links:
- 2023 IAS 12 Pillar Two Amendments
58. Q: What Pillar Two disclosures may be required before and after legislation takes effect?
A: Show answer
Before legislation is effective, an affected entity discloses known or reasonably estimable information about its exposure to Pillar Two income taxes arising from enacted or substantively enacted rules. If information is not known or estimable, explain that and describe progress in assessing exposure. Once legislation is effective, separately disclose current tax expense or income related to Pillar Two where required.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a jurisdictional assessment distinguishing pre-effective exposure from post-effective current tax."
Key point:
- Pillar Two disclosures change as local legislation becomes effective.
- The entity must explain exposure and separately identify current Pillar Two tax when required.
Source links:
- 2023 IAS 12 Pillar Two Amendments
59. Q: Why must tax calculations be performed separately for different jurisdictions?
A: Show answer
Tax rates, taxable-profit rules, loss restrictions, deduction timing, withholding taxes and incentives vary by jurisdiction. A single group-wide rate or schedule can misstate current and deferred tax. Identify the taxable entity and tax authority for each balance, apply local law and track losses and differences in the correct jurisdiction. Group offsetting is permitted only when legal and IAS 12 conditions are met.
Study instruction:
- "Segment the tax calculation by legal entity and jurisdiction and identify rate, tax-base and loss restrictions."
Key point:
- Income tax is jurisdiction-specific.
- Loss utilisation and offsetting depend on legal entity and tax authority.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
60. Q: Why is the chapter's 30 per cent rate not universal?
A: Show answer
The chapter uses 30 per cent for illustration, but actual rates are set by tax legislation and may vary by country, income type, entity status, distribution policy or manner of recovery. Some jurisdictions impose withholding taxes, minimum taxes or special incentives. Use the rate enacted or substantively enacted at reporting date and expected when differences reverse. A hardcoded example rate is not a substitute for tax-law analysis.
Study instruction:
- "Replace the example rate with the relevant rate for each taxable entity and document special rules."
Key point:
- The 30 per cent rate is illustrative only.
- Measurement must reflect jurisdictional law and expected reversal conditions.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
61. Q: How does the Iris Ltd example calculate current tax?
A: Show answer
The example starts with accounting profit of Â£250,450 and adjusts for non-deductible expenses, development deductions, tax depreciation, cash-paid insurance and leave, doubtful debts written off and rent received. Taxable profit is Â£137,567; at the illustrative 30 per cent rate, current tax is about Â£41,270. The method is to reconstruct ledger accounts where needed rather than assume accounting expense equals the tax deduction.
Study instruction:
- "Reperform the Iris Ltd current-tax worksheet and check taxable profit and the tax multiplication."
Key point:
- Current tax is calculated from taxable profit after adjustments.
- Ledger reconstructions identify cash-based deductions and reversals.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
62. Q: How does the Iris Ltd deferred-tax worksheet calculate closing balances?
A: Show answer
The worksheet compares carrying amounts and tax bases for receivables, prepaid insurance, rent receivable, development expenditure, equipment, goodwill and annual leave. It identifies taxable differences of Â£174,500 and deductible differences of Â£77,000, removes the Â£21,000 goodwill difference and applies 30 per cent. Closing DTL is Â£46,050 and closing DTA Â£23,100. Comparing opening and closing balances gives a Â£28,900 DTL increase and Â£1,800 DTA decrease.
Study instruction:
- "Rebuild the worksheet and reconcile differences to opening balances and the journal entry."
Key point:
- The worksheet calculates closing balances by asset and liability.
- Recognition exceptions and opening balances are applied before posting movement.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
63. Q: What does academic research suggest about book-tax differences and earnings quality?
A: Show answer
Research reviewed in the chapter suggests large differences between accounting and taxable profit can provide information about future earnings, cash flows and earnings quality. Some studies find taxable income relative to book income helps predict growth, while large or changing differences may relate to lower earnings persistence or credit ratings. These findings are context-dependent and do not prove manipulation. Analysts should identify whether differences arise from timing, tax incentives, jurisdictional rules or discretionary estimates.
Study instruction:
- "Classify a large book-tax difference and assess whether it reflects timing, law, growth or possible earnings-quality concerns."
Key point:
- Book-tax differences can contain information but require interpretation.
- A difference is not evidence of manipulation without analysis of cause and persistence.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
64. Q: How can deferred tax balances inform expectations of future tax payments?
A: Show answer
Deferred tax reflects future deductions or taxable amounts expected when assets are recovered and liabilities settled. Some DTAs, especially expenses recognised before tax deductions, may relate to lower future cash taxes. Other DTLs from accelerated depreciation may not cause a simple one-for-one cash-tax increase if new asset additions continuously create differences. Users should examine each source and reversal pattern rather than treat total deferred tax as a direct forecast of next year's tax payments.
Study instruction:
- "Separate deferred tax by source and prepare a reversal schedule to assess future tax cash flows."
Key point:
- Deferred tax can provide information about future tax consequences.
- Cash-flow implications depend on the type and reversal pattern of each difference.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
65. Q: How can management judgement affect DTA estimates and tax expense?
A: Show answer
DTA recoverability requires forecasts and judgement about future taxable profit, tax-planning opportunities and reversal timing. These judgements can materially affect tax expense and net assets, especially for entities with losses or volatile earnings. Under IFRS, recognition is based on probable utilisation; do not import US GAAP terminology such as a separate valuation allowance without explaining the framework difference. Forecasts should be supported and independently reviewed.
Study instruction:
- "Review a material DTA estimate and identify assumptions that could increase or reduce tax expense."
Key point:
- DTA recoverability is judgemental and can materially affect results.
- Use IFRS recognition criteria rather than terminology from another framework.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
66. Q: What controls reduce the risk of earnings management through income-tax accounting?
A: Show answer
Require independent review of tax-return adjustments, permanent and temporary difference schedules, tax-loss utilisation, rate changes, uncertain tax positions and DTA forecasts. Deferred-tax worksheets should reconcile to the ledger and prior-year balances, with documented reasons for movements. Tax reconciliations should be checked against returns and legal advice, while significant positions are reviewed independently of preparers. These controls reduce unsupported estimates and optimistic assumptions.
Study instruction:
- "Design a review checklist covering tax-return reconciliations, DTA recoverability, uncertain positions and deferred-tax movements."
Key point:
- Tax accounting is vulnerable to judgement and estimate bias.
- Independent review, evidence and reconciliations protect tax-expense integrity.
Source links:
- IFRIC 23 Uncertainty over Income Tax Treatments
67. Q: What should a tax close checklist include?
A: Show answer
Confirm taxable entities and jurisdictions, current-tax calculations, instalments, prior-year assessments, losses and credits, temporary differences, tax bases, DTA recognition, rate changes, uncertain treatments, OCI and equity effects, business combinations, offsetting and disclosures. Include reconciliations to the ledger, returns and supporting schedules, reviewer sign-off and follow-up of open matters. Each task should have an owner, due date and evidence reference.
Study instruction:
- "Convert the chapter into a close checklist with preparer, reviewer, evidence and status for each step."
Key point:
- The tax close covers current tax, deferred tax and disclosure.
- A controlled checklist creates a reproducible audit trail.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
68. Q: What is the practical sequence for analysing a tax difference under IAS 12?
A: Show answer
Identify the carrying amount and tax treatment. Determine the tax base by analysing future taxable benefits and deductions, calculate and classify the difference, apply recognition exceptions and assess probable profit for a DTA. Measure using the expected enacted or substantively enacted rate, recognise the effect in the same statement location as the underlying item and reconcile closing to opening balances. This sequence prevents unsupported journals.
Study instruction:
- "Apply the sequence to one asset and one liability and prepare a memo, worksheet and journal entry."
Key point:
- IAS 12 proceeds from carrying amount and tax base to recognition and measurement.
- The analysis ends with recognition location and reconciliation, not just a rate multiplication.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
69. Q: What are the most important conclusions from Chapter 15 on income taxes?
A: Show answer
IAS 12 requires current tax and future tax consequences to be recognised for transactions and balances, subject to exceptions. Permanent differences affect current tax but do not reverse; temporary differences arise from carrying amounts and tax bases and may create DTAs or DTLs. DTLs are generally recognised, while DTAs require probable future taxable profit. Tax effects follow the underlying item into profit or loss, OCI or equity, and detailed reconciliations and disclosures are required. Reliable reporting depends on jurisdiction-specific law, supported estimates and controlled close processes.
Study instruction:
- "Summarise the chapter as a workflow from taxable profit through tax bases, differences, recognition, measurement and disclosure."
Key point:
- IAS 12 connects current tax, deferred tax and tax consequences of recognised balances.
- Accurate tax accounting requires tax-law analysis, recoverability evidence and complete disclosure.
Source links:
- IAS 12 Income Taxes
Rows: 69
Table 16
Statement of Cash Flows: Classification, Preparation, and Analysis
1. Q: What is the purpose of a statement of cash flows?
A: Show answer
A statement of cash flows explains the historical movement in an entity's cash and cash equivalents during a reporting period. It classifies cash receipts and payments into operating, investing and financing activities, then reconciles the opening balance to the closing balance. It complements, rather than replaces, the statement of financial position and the statement of financial performance. The UN IPSAS Finance Manual includes a statement of cash flows in the complete set of financial statements and illustrates an indirect-method presentation for the UN. The governing framework and reporting-entity policy determine the precise presentation.
Study instruction:
- "Explain how the statement of cash flows complements the statement of financial position and the statement of financial performance."
Key point:
- It explains where cash came from, how it was used and how the closing balance was reached.
- It is a historical financial statement, not a cash budget or forecast.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
2. Q: Why is cash flow information useful even when an entity already reports a surplus or profit?
A: Show answer
Surplus or profit is measured on an accrual basis and can include revenue not yet collected, expenses not yet paid, non-cash charges and gains that do not represent operating receipts. An entity can therefore report a surplus while experiencing a cash shortage, for example when receivables rise, inventory is purchased in advance or suppliers are paid before grant receipts arrive. Conversely, depreciation or an impairment charge can reduce surplus without using cash in the current period. Cash flow information helps users assess liquidity, the ability to meet obligations, dependence on external financing and the sustainability of operations.
Study instruction:
- "Compare a reported surplus with operating cash flow and identify the accruals and non-cash items that explain any difference."
Key point:
- Accrual performance and cash availability answer different questions.
- A positive surplus does not by itself prove that an entity can pay its obligations when due.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
3. Q: What is the difference between cash and cash equivalents?
A: Show answer
Cash comprises cash on hand and demand deposits. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that can be converted readily into known amounts of cash and are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value. They are held to meet short-term cash commitments, not to earn a long-term investment return. The UN Finance Manual describes cash and cash equivalents as including bank and cash balances and qualifying short-term, highly liquid investments. An investment's label is not decisive: its maturity, convertibility, value risk and actual cash-management purpose must be assessed.
Study instruction:
- "Classify examples such as petty cash, a demand deposit, a 90-day deposit, listed shares and a long-term bond against the cash-equivalent criteria."
Key point:
- Cash equivalents must be highly liquid, readily convertible and low risk in value.
- An investment is not a cash equivalent merely because management expects to sell it soon.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 12: Cash Management and Cash Equivalents
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows
4. Q: How should the three-month maturity indicator be applied when assessing a cash equivalent?
A: Show answer
An investment will normally qualify only when it has a short maturity, commonly three months or less from the date of acquisition. The assessment is made from the acquisition date, not simply by looking at the remaining maturity at the reporting date. The short period supports the expectation that the amount convertible to cash is known and that value risk is insignificant. A longer-term deposit does not become a cash equivalent solely because only three months remain before maturity. The entity should document the original maturity, redemption terms, exposure to value changes and purpose for holding the instrument.
Study instruction:
- "For each deposit or money-market instrument, record its acquisition date, original maturity, redemption conditions and risk of value change."
Key point:
- The usual three-month indicator is measured from acquisition.
- Maturity is one criterion; liquidity, known value, insignificant risk and purpose also matter.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 12: Cash Management and Cash Equivalents
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows
5. Q: How should cash subject to donor, project or other restrictions be presented and disclosed?
A: Show answer
A restriction on how cash may be spent does not automatically mean that the balance ceases to be cash or a cash equivalent. The entity must assess whether it can access the deposit on demand, whether the restriction affects convertibility, and whether the balance is available for general use. The UN IPSAS framework requires disclosure in the notes of cash and cash equivalents that are not available for use, with additional information about the nature and substance of significant restrictions. Under IFRS, the IFRIC has also considered demand deposits that remain accessible on demand despite contractual restrictions on their use. Presentation and current/non-current classification require separate analysis.
Study instruction:
- "Review a restricted grant bank balance and distinguish the legal restriction, access to the deposit, cash-equivalent status and disclosure required."
Key point:
- Restricted use and cash-equivalent classification are related but separate assessments.
- Significant balances unavailable for general use require transparent disclosure.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- IFRS Interpretations Committee: November 2025 Update
6. Q: When can a bank overdraft be included in cash and cash equivalents?
A: Show answer
Under IAS 7, a bank overdraft is normally a financing activity rather than cash. It may be included as a component of cash and cash equivalents only when it is repayable on demand and forms an integral part of the entity's cash management. A characteristic arrangement is one in which the account regularly fluctuates between positive and overdrawn balances. A long-term borrowing facility or an overdraft used as a separate source of finance does not meet that test merely because the bank calls it an overdraft. IPSAS reporters should apply the current IPSAS requirements and their entity's approved policy rather than automatically importing an IFRS conclusion.
Study instruction:
- "Inspect the overdraft agreement, demand-repayment terms, actual account pattern and treasury purpose before deciding its treatment."
Key point:
- The IAS 7 exception is narrow and depends on both demand repayment and integration with cash management.
- A financing facility is not a cash equivalent simply because it is linked to a bank account.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
7. Q: Why are transfers between cash and cash equivalents excluded from the statement of cash flows?
A: Show answer
Transfers between items that already form part of cash and cash equivalents are movements within the entity's cash-management pool, not receipts from or payments to an outside activity. For example, transferring funds from a current account to a qualifying short-term deposit does not create a new operating, investing or financing cash flow. Reporting both sides would inflate gross movements without changing the aggregate cash and cash-equivalent balance. The UN IPSAS Policy Framework explicitly excludes movements between items making up cash or cash equivalents and the investment of excess cash in qualifying cash equivalents. The underlying investment must first satisfy the definition.
Study instruction:
- "Trace a transfer between a bank account and a short-term deposit and determine whether both balances qualify as cash equivalents."
Key point:
- Internal transfers within the defined cash-and-cash-equivalent pool are excluded.
- A purchase of an investment outside that pool may be an investing cash flow.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 12: Cash Management and Cash Equivalents
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
8. Q: What are the three activity categories in a statement of cash flows?
A: Show answer
Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing or service-delivery activities and other activities that are neither investing nor financing. Investing activities concern acquiring and disposing of long-term assets and investments that are not cash equivalents. Financing activities change the size or composition of contributed capital and borrowings. The categories help users understand whether cash is generated by operations, committed to resources for future service or returns, or obtained from and repaid to providers of finance. Classification must reflect the substance of the transaction and the reporting entity's applicable accounting framework.
Study instruction:
- "Create a classification list for routine receipts, supplier payments, asset purchases, asset disposals, borrowings and loan repayments."
Key point:
- Operating, investing and financing describe the nature of cash activity.
- A transaction's account name alone does not determine its cash-flow category.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
9. Q: Which cash receipts and payments are normally classified as operating activities?
A: Show answer
Operating cash flows generally arise from the activities that produce the entity's revenue or deliver its services. Examples include receipts from sales, service fees, grants, donations and appropriations intended to fund the UN's main programmes and operations, as well as payments to suppliers, employees and implementing partners when those payments finance operations rather than loans or asset acquisitions. Operating activities also include cash flows that do not meet the definitions of investing or financing. Classification should be consistent with the entity's main activities and the governing standard, not based solely on the budget code or donor label.
Study instruction:
- "Classify a sample of programme receipts, staff payments, partner transfers, supplier invoices and asset purchases using the applicable reporting policy."
Key point:
- Operating activities reflect the entity's principal operations and service delivery.
- For UN reporting, grants and donations funding main programmes are typical operating receipts.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Corporate Guidance: Reporting of Budget Information in Financial Statements
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
10. Q: Which cash flows are classified as investing activities?
A: Show answer
Investing activities generally include cash paid to acquire property, plant and equipment, intangible assets and other long-term resources, and cash received from their disposal. They can also include acquisitions and disposals of investments that are not cash equivalents, and loans made to or repaid by other parties when lending is not the entity's principal revenue-producing activity. The expenditure must result in a recognised asset to qualify as an investing cash flow under IAS 7. Research expenditure that is expensed rather than capitalised is therefore not transformed into investing activity merely because management expects future benefits.
Study instruction:
- "Review recent capital expenditure and investment transactions and link each cash movement to the asset or investment recognised in the ledger."
Key point:
- Investing cash flows show cash committed to or recovered from long-term resources and non-cash-equivalent investments.
- A payment that creates no recognised asset is not automatically an investing cash flow.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
11. Q: Which cash flows are classified as financing activities?
A: Show answer
Financing activities relate to changes in contributed equity and borrowings. Typical examples include cash received from new loans or bond issues, repayments of borrowed principal, proceeds from issuing shares or other equity instruments, and cash paid to redeem or buy back the entity's own equity. For a public-sector or NGO entity, the precise meaning of contributed capital and financing arrangements depends on its legal and funding structure. The statement should distinguish a new borrowing from a grant receipt and a repayment of loan principal from interest or service costs, using the applicable standard and policy.
Study instruction:
- "Separate the principal and any interest in a loan repayment and identify which financing balances changed during the period."
Key point:
- Financing cash flows explain how the entity obtains and repays capital and borrowings.
- A grant that funds ordinary programmes is not a borrowing merely because it is a major cash receipt.
Source links:

12. Q: How should a transaction containing more than one type of cash flow be classified?
A: Show answer
A single payment can contain components belonging to different activities. The UN IPSAS Policy Framework gives a loan repayment containing interest and principal as an example: the interest component may be classified as operating, while the principal component is financing. The cash-flow schedule should therefore split the transaction using the underlying contractual and accounting information rather than classify the entire bank payment to one category. The same discipline is needed for mixed settlements, asset purchases that include financing elements, or combined acquisition transactions. The split must be supported and applied consistently under the governing framework.
Study instruction:
- "Take a loan instalment and reconcile the bank payment to principal, interest, fees and any non-cash movement."
Key point:
- Classify the components of a mixed transaction separately when their nature differs.
- The bank statement shows the total payment, but the contract and ledger explain its components.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
13. Q: How should grants, donations and appropriations be classified in a UN or NGO statement of cash flows?
A: Show answer
The UN Corporate Guidance identifies cash receipts from grants, donations and other appropriations paid to fund the UN's main programmes and operations as operating cash flows. Cash paid to implementing partners to finance their operations is also an operating example, excluding loans. A transfer to acquire a controlled long-term asset or a genuine financing instrument may require a different analysis. Donor restrictions, project coding and the revenue-recognition treatment do not automatically determine the cash-flow category. Finance staff should document the purpose, contractual terms, recipient, accounting substance and the applicable reporting policy before classifying a material receipt or payment.
Study instruction:
- "Select three grant receipts and two partner transfers and explain why each is operating, investing or financing under the entity's policy."
Key point:
- Programme funding receipts are generally operating under the UN guidance.
- A donor restriction or project code does not by itself determine the cash-flow category.

- UN IPSAS Corporate Guidance: Reporting of Budget Information in Financial Statements
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
14. Q: What is the direct method of presenting operating cash flows?
A: Show answer
The direct method reports major classes of gross operating cash receipts and gross operating cash payments, such as cash collected from customers or donors, cash paid to suppliers and cash paid to employees. It focuses on actual cash movement rather than starting with accounting surplus or profit. The information may be obtained from cash records or reconstructed by adjusting income-statement amounts for movements in related receivables, payables, inventory, prepayments and accruals. IAS 7 encourages the direct method because gross receipt and payment information can assist users in estimating future cash flows. The applicable IPSAS framework also permits direct or indirect presentation.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare an operating cash-flow section using gross receipts and payments from bank and subledger records."
Key point:
- The direct method presents gross operating receipts and payments.
- It can provide useful visibility into the sources and uses of operating cash.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
15. Q: What is the indirect method of presenting operating cash flows?
A: Show answer
The indirect method begins with surplus or deficit, or the appropriate profit measure under the applicable framework, and adjusts it for non-cash items, working-capital movements and income or expenses whose cash effects belong to investing or financing activities. Depreciation, impairment and provisions may be added back because they reduced accounting performance without a corresponding current-period cash payment. Increases in operating receivables or inventory generally reduce operating cash, while increases in operating payables generally increase it. The UN IPSAS Policy Framework states that the UN uses the indirect method and illustrates this approach in the UN model financial statements.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile surplus or deficit to operating cash flow and explain each non-cash and working-capital adjustment."
Key point:
- The indirect method reconciles accrual performance to operating cash movement.
- Each adjustment must be supported by a clear explanation and reliable opening and closing balances.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows
16. Q: How do the direct and indirect methods differ, and do they produce different operating cash totals?
A: Show answer
The methods present the operating section differently, but when prepared correctly they reconcile to the same net cash flow from operating activities. The direct method shows gross receipts and payments. The indirect method starts from surplus or profit and adjusts for non-cash items, working-capital changes and items classified elsewhere. A direct presentation can make cash collection and payment patterns more visible; an indirect presentation explains why accrual performance differs from cash generation. The UN uses the indirect method, while IAS 7 permits both. The choice and required disclosures must follow the entity's reporting framework and policy.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare both presentations from the same trial balance, comparative statements and cash records, then reconcile their final operating cash totals."
Key point:
- The methods differ in presentation, not in the underlying cash generated.
- A reconciliation between the methods is a useful accuracy check.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
17. Q: How should changes in working capital be treated under the indirect method?
A: Show answer
Working-capital adjustments convert accrual revenue and expense into cash receipts and payments. An increase in trade receivables normally means some recognised revenue has not yet been collected, so it is deducted. An increase in inventory usually means cash was used to acquire goods not yet charged to cost of sales, so it is deducted. An increase in operating payables means some recognised expenses or purchases have not yet been paid, so it is added. Increases in prepayments generally use cash before expense recognition and are deducted; decreases in accruals can indicate that cash has been paid to settle earlier expenses.
Study instruction:
- "For each working-capital account, calculate the opening-to-closing movement and state why it increases or reduces cash."
Key point:
- Asset increases usually absorb operating cash; operating liability increases usually preserve cash temporarily.
- Analyse account movements and non-cash adjustments before applying a simple sign rule.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
18. Q: How can cash receipts from customers be calculated from sales revenue and receivables?
A: Show answer
A basic reconciliation is cash receipts = sales revenue + opening trade receivables â closing trade receivables. For example, sales revenue of 800,000 plus opening receivables of 70,000 less closing receivables of 79,000 gives receipts of 791,000. The calculation assumes no other non-cash changes. Discounts allowed, write-offs, foreign-exchange movements, acquisitions, reclassifications and impairment adjustments may need separate analysis so that the balancing figure is not mistaken for cash. The receivables control account should reconcile opening balance, invoices, credit notes, cash collected and closing balance.
Study instruction:
- "Reconstruct the receivables account and reconcile the calculated receipts to bank credits and remittance information."
Key point:
- Opening receivables are added and closing receivables are deducted from sales revenue.
- Non-cash changes must be identified before treating the balancing figure as cash collected.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
19. Q: How are cash payments to inventory suppliers calculated under the direct method?
A: Show answer
First calculate purchases: cost of sales â opening inventory + closing inventory. Then calculate cash paid to suppliers: purchases + opening trade payables â closing trade payables, with adjustments for discounts received, credit notes, non-cash acquisitions, foreign exchange and other relevant movements. In the chapter's illustration, cost of sales of 480,000, opening inventory of 65,000 and closing inventory of 70,000 produce purchases of 485,000. Adding opening payables of 42,000 and deducting closing payables of 45,000 gives cash payments of 482,000 before any further adjustments.
Study instruction:
- "Build separate inventory and supplier-payable reconciliations and agree the resulting cash payment to bank transactions."
Key point:
- Cost of sales must be adjusted for inventory movements to derive purchases.
- Purchases must then be adjusted for payable movements to derive cash paid.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
20. Q: How are cash payments for services and employee costs calculated?
A: Show answer
For service expenses, adjust the accrual expense for prepayments and accrued liabilities. In the chapter's illustration, other expenses of 76,000, opening prepayments of 8,000, closing prepayments of 9,500, opening accrued expenses of 3,000 and closing accrued expenses of 1,800 produce service payments of 78,700. Employee payments can be calculated as wage expense + opening wages payable â closing wages payable. With wage expense of 120,000, opening payable of 4,000 and closing payable of 5,000, cash paid is 119,000. Other non-cash or reclassification movements must be separately identified.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile service expenses and payroll costs to prepayments, accruals, payroll registers and bank payments."
Key point:
- Prepayments and accruals explain the timing difference between expense and cash paid.
- Payroll and supplier payments should be supported by separate reconciliations.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
21. Q: Which non-cash items commonly require adjustment when preparing operating cash flows?
A: Show answer
Common adjustments include depreciation, amortisation, impairment, provisions, non-cash employee-benefit costs, unrealised foreign-exchange gains or losses and other accruals that affected surplus or profit without creating a current-period cash flow. Under the indirect method, non-cash expenses are generally added back and non-cash gains generally deducted, subject to the nature of the item and the framework. The UN model statement identifies depreciation, amortisation, impairment, allowance movements and several employee-benefit and joint-venture items. The preparer should trace each adjustment to the supporting schedule rather than insert a balancing figure without explanation.
Study instruction:
- "Identify each non-cash item in the statement of financial performance and trace it to the relevant asset, liability or supporting schedule."
Key point:
- Non-cash adjustments remove accounting effects that do not represent current-period cash movement.
- The direction of an adjustment depends on whether it increased or reduced accrual performance.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
22. Q: Why are gains and losses on the disposal of long-term assets adjusted in the indirect method?
A: Show answer
A gain or loss on disposal affects accounting performance, but the cash proceeds from selling the asset are classified as investing activity. To avoid including the disposal result in operating cash flow, the indirect method removes the gain from profit or adds back the loss, then reports the actual proceeds in investing activities. For example, if equipment with a carrying amount of 10,000 is sold for 14,000, the gain is 4,000. The gain is deducted from the indirect operating reconciliation and the 14,000 cash receipt is shown as an investing inflow.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile an asset-disposal journal to carrying amount, accumulated depreciation, gain or loss and cash proceeds."
Key point:
- The gain or loss is an accrual-performance adjustment, not the disposal cash flow.
- Report actual proceeds in investing activities when the asset disposal qualifies as investing.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
23. Q: How should interest and dividends received or paid be classified and disclosed?
A: Show answer
Classification depends on the reporting framework and the period's applicable requirements. IAS 7 historically allowed interest and dividends received and paid to be classified consistently as operating, investing or financing, with separate disclosure; the UN IPSAS model statement also requires interest received and paid to be disclosed separately. The UN IPSAS Policy Framework gives examples in which interest and principal components of a loan repayment may fall into different categories. Preparers must not assume that the IFRS policy choices automatically apply to an IPSAS reporter. Document the selected policy, apply it consistently and check amendments effective for the reporting period.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the entity's accounting policy with the governing standard and trace interest and dividend cash flows separately."
Key point:
- Separate disclosure and consistent classification are essential.
- Do not transfer an IFRS classification choice into an IPSAS report without checking the applicable rule.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows
24. Q: How should income tax payments be presented in the statement of cash flows?
A: Show answer
Under IAS 7, income taxes paid are separately disclosed and classified as operating unless they can be specifically identified with investing or financing activities. The tax expense recognised in profit or loss may not equal cash tax paid because of current tax payable movements, deferred tax, prior-year settlements and tax effects recognised outside profit or loss. A preparer may need to reconstruct current and deferred tax balances to isolate the cash payment. Public-sector and NGO entities may have different tax profiles, such as payroll withholding or indirect taxes, so the applicable law, entity policy and reporting framework must be checked.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile current tax expense, deferred tax movements, tax payable and cash remittances for the reporting period."
Key point:
- Tax expense and tax paid are different measures.
- Separate tax disclosures and classification should follow the applicable standard and facts.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
25. Q: How are cash flows from obtaining or losing control of a subsidiary presented?
A: Show answer
Under IAS 7, the aggregate cash flows from obtaining or losing control of subsidiaries and other businesses are presented separately within investing activities. The net cash flow on acquisition deducts cash and cash equivalents acquired from the cash consideration paid. On disposal, cash and cash equivalents held by the business disposed of are deducted from cash consideration received. The notes also provide information about total consideration, the cash component, cash acquired or disposed of and major categories of other assets and liabilities. The consolidated statement should not obscure the scale of these transactions by combining acquisitions and disposals into an unexplained net figure.
Study instruction:
- "For a business acquisition or disposal, reconcile consideration, cash acquired or disposed of and the net investing cash flow."
Key point:
- Acquisition and disposal cash flows are separately identified and adjusted for cash held by the business.
- Non-cash consideration and other acquired assets and liabilities require supporting disclosures.
Source links:
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
26. Q: How should non-cash investing and financing transactions be treated?
A: Show answer
Transactions such as acquiring an asset by assuming a lease liability, converting debt to equity or acquiring an asset through a non-cash contribution do not involve current cash receipts or payments. They are excluded from the statement of cash flows, but the UN IPSAS Policy Framework and IAS 7 require relevant information to be disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements. Excluding them from the cash-flow statement does not make them unimportant: they can materially change assets, liabilities, financing structure and future cash commitments. The preparer should identify the transaction, document its non-cash nature and ensure that the relevant balance-sheet and note disclosures are complete.
Study instruction:
- "Review major investing and financing journals and identify which transactions changed balances without moving cash."
Key point:
- Only actual movements in cash and cash equivalents appear as cash flows.
- Material non-cash investing and financing transactions still require disclosure.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
27. Q: How should cash flows denominated in a foreign currency be translated?
A: Show answer
Foreign-currency cash flows are translated into the reporting or functional currency using the exchange rate applicable at the date of the cash flow, or an appropriate rate that approximates actual transaction-date rates where the standard permits. The UN IPSAS Policy Framework specifies use of the UN Operational Rate of Exchange for its reporting context. A period average may be appropriate only when it reasonably approximates the rates on the actual transaction dates and exchange rates have not fluctuated significantly. A closing rate should not be applied indiscriminately to all cash receipts and payments. Keep the source currency, transaction date, rate and translated amount in the audit trail.
Study instruction:
- "Select a sample of foreign-currency receipts and payments and recalculate the reporting-currency amount using the approved rate source."
Key point:
- Translate cash flows using transaction-date rates or a permitted reasonable approximation.
- The approved exchange-rate policy and reporting currency must be documented.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
28. Q: Why is the effect of exchange-rate changes on foreign-currency cash shown separately?
A: Show answer
Unrealised exchange gains and losses are not cash receipts or payments. However, exchange-rate changes affect the reporting-currency value of foreign-currency cash and cash equivalents between the beginning and end of the period. The statement therefore presents the effect of exchange-rate changes separately from operating, investing and financing cash flows so that the opening-to-closing reconciliation works. The UN IPSAS Policy Framework makes this distinction explicitly. The preparer should separate exchange differences on cash balances from realised cash flows and from exchange gains or losses on other monetary assets and liabilities.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile foreign-currency cash by currency, separating actual cash movements from the exchange-rate effect on opening and closing balances."
Key point:
- Exchange-rate effects on cash are not operating, investing or financing receipts or payments.
- A separate reconciling line explains the reporting-currency movement in cash balances.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
29. Q: How should the statement of cash flows reconcile opening and closing cash and cash equivalents?
A: Show answer
The reconciliation starts with cash and cash equivalents at the beginning of the period, adds or subtracts net operating, investing and financing cash flows, and then includes the separately presented exchange-rate effect on foreign-currency cash. The result must equal cash and cash equivalents at the end of the period. The ending figure should agree with the related amount in the statement of financial position and with the supporting cash and investment schedules. Any difference may indicate an omitted bank account, an incorrect cash-equivalent classification, an unrecorded transaction, a translation error or a cut-off problem.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare the opening-to-closing bridge and agree both endpoints to the general ledger and statement of financial position."
Key point:
- The closing cash figure must reconcile to the reported balance-sheet amount.
- An unexplained difference is a control exception, not a rounding adjustment to hide.

- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements

30. Q: What disclosures should explain the components of cash and cash equivalents?
A: Show answer
The notes should identify the material components of cash and cash equivalents and reconcile them to the statement of financial position. Depending on the entity, this may include cash on hand, bank accounts, demand deposits, qualifying short-term deposits and cash-pool balances. Significant balances unavailable for general use should be described, including the nature of the restriction and why the cash cannot be used for ordinary operations. The UN model financial statements provide a note structure for cash pools and other cash equivalents. Disclosures should be tailored to the actual facts and avoid leaving template placeholders or unexplained aggregate balances.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile each component in the cash note to bank confirmations, cash counts, deposit schedules and the general ledger."
Key point:
- The note should make the composition and availability of cash understandable.
- Material restrictions and unavailable balances must not be hidden within a single total.

- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures

31. Q: How should United Nations cash-pool balances be assessed for cash-flow reporting?
A: Show answer
The UN Treasury pools cash from participating entities and invests the combined funds while maintaining liquidity and managing risk. The Finance Manual explains that cash-pool holdings may be presented as cash and cash equivalents, short-term investments or long-term investments depending on maturity and classification. The UN IPSAS framework distinguishes movements within cash and cash equivalents, which are excluded, from cash flows relating to investments outside that pool. A participant should use its recognised share, approved treasury reports and the governing classification policy. It should not assume every cash-pool unit is automatically a cash equivalent regardless of maturity.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile the entity's cash-pool share to treasury confirmations and classify each component by maturity and approved accounting policy."
Key point:
- Cash-pool classification depends on the instrument's nature and maturity.
- Transfers within cash equivalents differ from purchases or disposals of other investments.

32. Q: What source records are normally needed to prepare a reliable statement of cash flows?
A: Show answer
Preparation normally uses comparative statements of financial position, the statement of financial performance, the general ledger, bank statements, cash books, bank reconciliations, investment schedules and supporting transaction details. Additional information is needed to distinguish purchases from cost of sales, disposals from depreciation, new borrowings from repayments, cash dividends from non-cash distributions, and cash movements from reclassifications. The chapter explains that the statement is not simply extracted from a trial balance: balances and performance figures must be analysed and reconstructed. The preparer should maintain a documented link from each statement line to its underlying ledger accounts and evidence.
Study instruction:
- "Create a source-data checklist and trace each cash-flow line to the records needed to calculate and verify it."
Key point:
- The statement is prepared from reconciled financial statements plus transaction-level supporting information.
- A trial balance alone does not explain the cash effect of every accrual or balance movement.
Source links:
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
- IPSASB: 2026 Handbook of International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board Pronouncements
33. Q: How can ledger-account reconstructions help identify cash receipts and payments?
A: Show answer
A reconstructed account uses opening and closing balances together with income, expense and non-cash movements to derive the missing cash amount as a balancing figure. For example, the receivables account reconciles opening receivables, credit sales, write-offs, discounts, cash receipts and closing receivables. Inventory and payables accounts can similarly identify purchases and supplier payments. This method is useful when direct cash information is not already grouped by activity. It is only reliable when all material non-cash entries, reclassifications, foreign-exchange effects and acquisition or disposal movements have been identified and supported.
Study instruction:
- "Reconstruct one receivables account and one payables account, then agree the derived cash figure to bank and subledger evidence."
Key point:
- A balancing cash figure is valid only after all other movements are explained.
- Reconstructed accounts provide an audit trail from accrual balances to cash.

- IFRS Foundation: IAS 7 Issued Standard (2024)
- UN IPSAS Policy Framework, IPSAS 2: Cash Flow Statements
- UN IPSAS Finance Manual, Chapter 16: Presentation of Financial Statements and Disclosures
34. Q: How should a statement of cash flows be prepared when comparative balances include revaluations, disposals or other non-cash movements?
A: Show answer
A simple difference between opening and closing balances is not necessarily a cash flow. A property balance may change because of purchases, disposals, depreciation, impairment, revaluation or a non-cash donation. A borrowing balance may change because of cash advances, repayments, lease recognition, foreign exchange or reclassification. The preparer must analyse the movement and isolate the cash components. Supporting asset registers, disposal forms, valuation schedules, financing agreements and journal entries help separate cash and non-cash changes. The statement should report only the cash component in the relevant activity and disclose material non-cash transactions separately.
Study instruction:
- "Choose an asset and a borrowing balance and prepare a movement schedule that separates cash and non-cash changes."
Key point:
- Opening-to-closing balance movements are not automatically cash flows.
- Every material movement should be analysed before classification.
